verdict.reasoning: Transcript: 3-day history of diarrhea (“It was three days ago”), initially watery then very loose, with vomiting and feeling feverish (“serious diarrhoea… started as being very watery… very loose”; “I've been running a serious temperature. I'm literally boiling”; extensive vomiting described).
Patient says she has lost count of bowel motions and had at least four today: “I lost count… Today alone, I've been at least four time.”

Patient reports vomiting everything including water and tea, and last episode ~2 hours ago after breakfast: “I've been throwing up… Not even water, not even my tea… I've just been throwing up everything.” and “I was sick just after trying… breakfast this morning, so maybe about two hours ago.”

Pain is periumbilical and associated with urge to defecate: “towards my navel area… It's just so sore. And it gets… it's almost like the center of my navel.” and “When it comes, I feel this strong urge to go to the… loo.” This supports intermittent periumbilical pain preceding defecation.
Doctor asks about blood in stool or urine; patient denies: “And any blood in the stool or in the urine that you've noticed?” Patient: “No blood.”

Urination 1 hour ago and color not observed are explicit: “And when did you last pass urine…?” Patient: “an hour ago.” and “To be honest, I have a look so I really couldn't say.” Transcript does not report reduced frequency, so ‘normal frequency’ is a reasonable inference.

Patient has been in contact with brother who has similar symptoms and mentions a school-wide illness: “my brother… has actually been having similar symptoms… and he does say like everyone in school's got this.” and confirms contact: Doctor: “So you've been in contact with him, have you?” Patient: “Yes.”

No other medical/surgical history; only menstrual cramps mentioned: Doctor: “any surgery before, or abdominal problems, or any other medical issues?” Patient: “apart from the fact that this one is giving me abdominal pains, no previous abdominal pains before. Obviously I get the odd… menstrual cramps…” No other conditions are listed.

Daily vitamin D and PRN ibuprofen are explicit: “I take my… vitamin D, every day… For my menstrual cramps… I might take… an ibuprofen.” ORS frequency is “three times a day for the past two days,” which approximates every 8 hours; “I've taken that, like, um, three times a day for the past two days.”
Occupation, working from home, and household are explicit: “A graphics designer.”; “I've had to actually work from home today”; “I live with my brother and my mum.”

Smoking, alcohol, and drug use documented: “Well, I don't smoke, but, you know, I have a pint from time to time.” and “Do you take any other drugs? Patient: No. Like I said, I only take, um, vitamins.”

LMP, contraception, and intercourse status explicit: “when was your last period? Patient: Um, two weeks ago.”; “Are you on any contraception? Patient: No.”; “Are you having regular sexual intercourse? Patient: No.”

Doctor’s impression and symptoms support acute infectious gastroenteritis with dehydration risk: “it sounds like it might be some, an infectious gastroenteritis that you've got”; ongoing diarrhea, vomiting, fever described, and dehydration concern: “we should also check that you're not getting dehydrated, because if you're not keeping fluid down, then you can get dehydrated.”

Urgent appointment for hydration assessment and stool testing is planned: “we can make you an urgent appointment… you can get the sample sent off and we can check your hydration.” and “get a sample of the stool, so we can make sure that you haven't got a nasty bacterial infection.”
ORS continuation with tiny frequent sips is explicitly advised: “keep drinking, keep going with the rehydration salts. Just tiny sips constantly… just tiny, tiny sips but just keep going with it.”
Bland diet and foods to avoid are explicit: “just have very simple food… like toast or biscuit… Avoid, um, fruit, vegetables, uh, milk, anything like that, which might just make it worse.”

Transcript only states: “if, in the meantime, you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in A and E.” Specific red flags (increasing vomiting, reduced urine, dizziness, worsening pain/fever) are not mentioned.

Patient is told to book via support line and can call back: “So you'll have to book an appointment through the support line.” and “So you can call us back in the meantime.” This supports calling support line to book and follow-up as needed.
